output:
**Subject: The Knocknacarra reading club — some good news, and something I should have said first**

Dear Niamh,

I hope you're well. I wanted to write before the review meeting on Wednesday 18th, for two reasons: there's news I think you'll be glad of, and there's something I should have mentioned to you first and didn't.

The club has taken off. When we started in September we had five children most weeks, and that was what you were seeing when you wrote on 30th October about pausing from January. Since then: nine most weeks by mid-October, and fourteen children last Tuesday, 3rd November. That isn't a one good week, it feels like a real change in what the session is worth to the families who come. I wanted you to have those figures before the 18th so that you can look at the pause again with them in front of you, because I think pausing now would be a great pity, just as it's begun to work.

Part of it, plainly, is the books. Declan Moran at Salthill Book Nook gave us a hundred and twenty of them, mostly for the six to nine year olds and a good few in Gaeilge, and that's made a visible difference to what we can offer. But the part that strikes me most is the children themselves. Two sisters from a Ukrainian family joined us in October, and now the older one reads to the younger in English at the end of every session — that has quietly become one of the nicest things I have seen in a classroom, and it's not something I put there. And last week a lad who wouldn't open a book in September asked if he could take two home with him. I didn't name him, and I won't, but I wanted you to know the session is doing something.

Which brings me to the other reason I'm writing.

At the farmers' market I met Orla Keane from the Corrib Courier, and I got carried away and told her she was very welcome to come along any Tuesday. I know that has to come through you, and I know the policy: no photographs of children without your sign-off and the parental consent forms in place. I should have said "let me check with the coordinator" before I said anything at all, and I didn't. I was wrong, plain and simple, and I'm sorry — not because it's a big thing, but because it's left you with a decision to make on a subject you'd already told me needed your hand.

So here's what I'd like to do. I'll ring Orla and put the visit on hold until you have looked at it and decided — she's pencilled in for Tuesday 24th with a photographer, and I can tell her that's not going ahead until you've said so. Nothing happens before that. And if you do think a visit could work, I'd be glad to get the consent forms in myself. I know nearly all the families and I'm sure I can have them signed and back well before the 24th.

The coverage could be wonderful for us. But only if it's done properly, and properly means your sign-off and the forms, and if you think it isn't right then it isn't — I won't push you on it.

One other thing: if the hall insurance is the part of the pause that's hardest to shift, do say. I'd rather know what the sticking point is than guess at it.

Thank you for listening to all this, Niamh. I'd love it if the numbers could change your mind on the 18th, but whatever you decide, I'll be there on Tuesdays either way.

With warm regards,
[Your name]
Knocknacarra reading club volunteer, Tuesdays 3.30–4.45, meeting room upstairs, Knocknacarra Library
